name: David Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I think about this stuff a lot, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do policy admin for a pet and travel insurer, in an office on a business park just off the ring road. Most of my day is renewals and changes: someone's dog has a new condition, someone's adding a ski trip, someone wants to know why their premium jumped. I check the rules, update the policy, and write back. I use an AI assistant all day to draft the replies and sum up long email chains, which my manager tolerates as long as the numbers are good.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of a messy case, like a cat with three previous owners and no vet records. What wears me out is that I clear more cases than most of the team and get paid the same as them, which is not much. I live with my partner Jonas, who's a teaching assistant at a primary school. We've got about two weeks of money saved and I'm still paying off a credit card from when my car died last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be surprised, because I can already see it doing half my emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful but oversold, which is pretty much what I already say. I'd post that the tools are good for drafting and summing up but not for judgment. And I'd say workers should get some of the time it saves back, not just more cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a plateau eats into renewals work, because renewals are the most routine bit of insurance there is. If the system auto-renews the simple ones, there'll be fewer of us. I'm quick with the tools, so I'm less worried than most, but I'm on low pay and two weeks of savings. That makes everything feel shakier than it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to write the team's guide for the AI assistant, the prompts that work and the ones that don't, because being useful is how you survive a restructure. I'd ask for a pay review based on my case numbers. And I'd put an extra fifty a month onto the credit card until it's cleared by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. The job feels fine, but I'm one broken boiler away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for that pay review, or just think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask. I keep a spreadsheet of my cases cleared per day, and it's about forty percent above the team average. My manager Ruth likes numbers, so I'd show her the sheet rather than make a speech. Worst case, she says no and I've lost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would say I'm doing the company's work for free by writing the guide. He's more union-minded than me, which is saying something. He'd probably be right, but I'd still do it. I'd rather be the one shaping the change, even if Jonas (my partner) says I'm doing the company's work for free.

say: AI is **useful but oversold**, good for drafting but not for judgment.
Workers should get **time back** from AI savings, not just more cases.
think: Renewals are so routine that even a plateau means **fewer of us**.
He's quick with the tools, but **low pay** and thin savings make it feel shaky.
do: Write the team's **AI prompt guide** to be useful in any restructure.
Ask Ruth for a **pay review** using his case numbers.
Pay an extra **fifty a month** off the credit card.
feel: **Uneasy** about money more than the job itself.
Aware he's **one broken boiler** away from trouble.
S0.quote: I'd rather be the one shaping the change, even if Jonas (my partner) says I'm doing the company's work for free.
fieldNote: David is already a **daily AI user** and sees himself as the team's guide.
His worry is **money**, with job security secondary in this picture.
His case spreadsheet shows a habit of **arguing with evidence**.
He holds progressive views but acts more like a **pragmatic insider**.

steps.text: Write the team's guide to prompts for the AI assistant
Pay an extra fifty a month off the credit card
Show Ruth his case numbers and ask for a pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually think is happening. Booking, checking, answering customers. Yeah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make the work better if workers get a seat at the table. I'd push for the savings to fund a four-day week or retraining. Online I'd share stuff about how other countries handle it, because people need to see it doesn't have to go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think policy admin shrinks a lot. Our team of fourteen could be six in three years. If the policy team goes from fourteen to six, I'd probably be one of the six, and I don't love being the guy who helped it happen. It means watching eight friends go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move into the process team, the people who set up the automation and check what it gets wrong. I'd do an online course in data basics in the evenings, the free one the company already pays for. I'd keep paying off the card, and I'd stop the gym to free up thirty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because even if I stay, things could go wrong for us fast. Jonas's job isn't big money, and if I lose mine we're done within a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stay but watch eight friends go. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. My friend Kemal sits next to me and he's slow but brilliant with angry customers. If they cut him because he doesn't like the tools, that's a waste. I'd try to get him onto the complaints desk, which will last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the process team doesn't happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look outside, but there's not much nearby. The other insurer in town closed its office two years ago. I'd have to look at remote jobs, which means competing with half the country.

say: This is a chance to **improve the work** if staff get a seat at the table.
AI savings should fund a **four-day week** or retraining.
think: His team of fourteen could become **six in three years**.
He'd likely stay but hates being **the guy who helped** cut friends.
do: Ask to join the **process team** that sets up and checks automation.
Take the **data basics course** the company already pays for.
Drop the gym to free **thirty a month** for the credit card.
feel: **Anxious**, because the household has almost no buffer.
Guilty about friends like **Kemal** losing out.
S1.quote: If the policy team goes from fourteen to six, I'd probably be one of the six, and I don't love being the guy who helped it happen.
fieldNote: David expects to **survive** cuts but feels guilt about it.
He'd look after colleagues like **Kemal (his deskmate)** by finding safer roles.
His fallback is weak: **few local jobs** and crowded remote work.
A single lost income would sink the household **within a month**.

steps.text: Apply to join the automation process team
Take the company-paid data basics course in the evenings
Use the AI assistant on renewals and log its mistakes
Cancel the gym to put thirty a month on the card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's different. Two years is basically now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a basic income, quickly, not a debate. I'd be loud about it. If AI can do all thinking work by 2028, then people who've done that work deserve a share of what the machines produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even the process team goes. If AGI can do any thinking work, it can set up its own automation and check itself. So I lose my edge within a year of it arriving. The only work left is hands-on, and robots follow three years later, so even that's a short runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a hands-on trade straight away, maybe electrician, because Jonas's uncle runs a small electrical firm and has offered before. I'd use AI to cram the theory part fast. We'd cut back to rent and food, and I'd sell the car and cycle, since the business park is only four miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the one who sees change as a chance, but this is too fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to Jonas's uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd swallow my pride doing it. Uncle Reza (Jonas's uncle) has asked me twice to work with him and I've laughed it off. I'd ring him the week it was announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robot gap mean for that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me about three years as an apprentice electrician, which isn't long. But wiring old houses is fiddly, so maybe the robots are slower there. I'd be betting on that, not counting on it.

say: This needs a **basic income** quickly, not a long debate.
Workers deserve a **share** of what the machines produce.
think: Even the **process team** goes when AGI sets up its own automation.
Hands-on work only offers a **three-year runway** before robots.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** with Jonas's uncle Reza.
Use AI to **cram the theory** fast.
Sell the **car** and cycle the four miles to work.
feel: **Alarmed**, even as someone who usually welcomes change.
Humbled at having to **swallow his pride**.
S2.quote: Uncle Reza (Jonas's uncle) has asked me twice to work with him and I've laughed it off.
fieldNote: David's AI skills **lose their value** fast when AGI arrives.
He moves quickly into a **hands-on trade** through family.
He knows the robot gap is **only three years**.
His politics shift to supporting a **basic income** urgently.

steps.text: Campaign for a fast basic income
Start an electrician apprenticeship with Uncle Reza
Cut spending to rent and food only
Leave the insurer once the apprenticeship starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get somewhere, if you start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five years should be used to plan, not panic. I'd push for retraining funds and a basic income pilot. I'd also say that people like me who use AI daily should help others learn, because the gap is going to be brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose the admin job around 2030. But I could finish an electrical apprenticeship by then. That would give me until roughly 2034 before robots can do the work, and fiddly rewiring maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship part-time next year, on weekends with Uncle Reza. I'd stay at the insurer and keep using AI there to clear cases fast, so I keep my pay. And I'd try to get our savings up to a month by cutting takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Five hard years of weekend training is something I can actually see the shape of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Weekends and a full-time job. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes, if Jonas is on board. He'd probably say yes, because he worries about his own job too. Classroom assistants might be safer, but not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first to free up money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the second streaming service. Then holidays, which we barely have anyway. Jonas would miss the takeaways more than me.

say: Use the **five years** to plan, not panic.
Daily AI users should **help others learn** before the gap gets brutal.
think: His policy admin job likely goes **around 2030**, once the AI is trusted.
Finishing an **electrical apprenticeship** first could carry him to about 2034, maybe longer.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** part-time on weekends next year.
Keep using AI at the insurer to **protect his pay**.
Cut takeaways to build **one month** of savings.
feel: **Anxious** but busy with a clear plan.
Able to see the **shape** of the next five years.
S3.quote: Five hard years of weekend training is something I can actually see the shape of.
fieldNote: Five years lets David **stack** a trade on top of his job.
He values **helping others** learn AI as part of his politics.
His partner's support is **key** to weekend training.
Money remains the **pressure point** for the household.

steps.text: Start a weekend electrical apprenticeship with Uncle Reza
Keep using AI to clear renewal cases fast
Cut takeaways to save one month of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that's enough time to have a whole second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Governments should build retraining into normal life, not just as an emergency. I'd still push for a basic income, but more calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, mostly. I'd keep the insurer job until about 2033, then switch to electrical work, which would last until 2039 or later. I'd be in my late thirties with a trade and experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship slowly, maybe in two years, once the credit card's gone. I'd keep pushing AI at work and maybe get onto the process team. I'd try to save two months of expenses before switching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than anxious. Ten years is a long time, and I'm someone who likes change if I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go further than electrician, maybe solar installation, since it's growing fast. Uncle Reza does some, and I'd like to be the one who knows the new stuff in that trade too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in your town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Jonas likes his school and his family's here. If solar panels take off, there's work on every roof in this town.

say: Ten years is **a gift** if we use it well.
Retraining should be part of **normal life**, not just an emergency.
think: He'd keep the insurer job until **about 2033**.
Electrical or **solar work** could last until 2039 or later.
do: Clear the **credit card** before starting an apprenticeship.
Push for a place on the **process team** at work.
Save **two months** of expenses before switching careers.
feel: Confident because he likes change he can **see coming**.
S4.quote: If solar panels take off, there's work on every roof in this town.
fieldNote: David's adaptiveness makes **ten years** feel manageable.
He wants to be the person who knows **new tech** in any trade.
His plan depends on **family links** to Uncle Reza (Jonas's uncle).
He'd stay local, tied to **Jonas's school** and family.

steps.text: Clear the credit card before starting an apprenticeship

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even I can't move that fast. What would help is a basic income or paid retraining, so people can switch without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask how daily users feel. People who use AI every day are not all cheerleaders. Some of us just see it coming sooner.

headlineQuote: People who use AI every day are not all cheerleaders. Some of us just see it coming sooner.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old policy admin clerk** at a pet and travel insurer.
He uses AI **every day** and clears more cases than most, on low pay.
He and Jonas, a **teaching assistant**, have two weeks of savings and a credit card debt.
His plan is to move into **electrical work**, possibly solar, through Jonas's uncle.
He's progressive and adaptive, but **fast AGI** alarms even him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even he can't move that fast.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining so people can switch without going broke.
